case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician 4 months after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery because of palpitations, heat intolerance, and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss over 3 weeks. She stopped breastfeeding 6 weeks ago. She has no neck pain. Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/70 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is slightly enlarged, firm, and nontender. There is no proptosis. Laboratory studies show a TSH concentration below 0.01 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 of 3.0 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 10 mm/h (0 to 20). The 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake is 2% (10 to 30). The diagnosis is postpartum painless thyroiditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her thyroid disorder began in the months after delivery?
options: Viral injury of follicles with granulomatous inflammation
Ongoing stimulation of TSH receptors by placental hCG
Rebound autoimmunity after pregnancy-related tolerance
IgG4-related fibroinflammatory replacement of the gland
approach: Note the clues: a painless, nontender gland, a normal ESR, and thyrotoxicosis with very low radioiodine uptake 4 months after delivery.
Low uptake with high free T4 means stored hormone is leaking from damaged follicles, not being newly made.
A painless destructive thyroiditis after delivery is lymphocytic and autoimmune. It appears when the immune tolerance of pregnancy ends.
questions.why: Pregnancy dampens maternal immune responses so that the fetus is tolerated. After delivery this suppression lifts, and women with underlying thyroid autoimmunity, most of whom have antibodies to thyroid peroxidase, can develop a burst of lymphocytic inflammation in the gland. The inflamed follicles release stored hormone, causing a short thyrotoxic phase with low radioiodine uptake, often followed by a hypothyroid phase. Most women recover normal function within about a year, but some later develop permanent hypothyroidism. The painless gland and normal ESR separate it from subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, and the lack of a hard, fixed gland separates it from Riedel thyroiditis.
whyNot: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and causes a painful, tender gland with a high ESR. Her gland is painless and her ESR is normal.

hCG can weakly stimulate TSH receptors in early pregnancy, especially when levels are very high. It falls to very low levels within a few weeks after delivery, and receptor stimulation would raise radioiodine uptake, not lower it.
Correct.

IgG4-related (Riedel) thyroiditis replaces the gland with dense fibrosis, making it rock-hard and fixed to nearby structures, usually with normal or low thyroid function. It is not linked to pregnancy and does not cause sudden thyrotoxicosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following serum antibodies is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Antibodies to thyroid peroxidase
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins
Antibodies to 21-hydroxylase
Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase
approach: Painless destructive thyroiditis after pregnancy is a lymphocytic, autoimmune process closely related to Hashimoto thyroiditis.
The marker antibodies of this process target thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin.
Her very low radioiodine uptake argues against antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor.
questions.why: In Hashimoto thyroiditis and its painless and postpartum variants, the main injury comes from T cells. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill follicular cells, and cytokines such as interferon-gamma add to the damage. Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are found in most patients and are used to make the diagnosis, because they show that the gland is under autoimmune attack. Women who have anti-TPO antibodies early in pregnancy have a higher risk of postpartum thyroiditis and of later permanent hypothyroidism. In long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis, chronic lymphoid stimulation also raises the risk of thyroid B cell lymphoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins cause Graves disease, which can also begin after delivery. They drive new hormone synthesis, so radioiodine uptake would be high, not 2%.
Antibodies to 21-hydroxylase mark autoimmune Addison disease. They can occur alongside thyroid autoimmunity but do not explain her thyroid disorder.
Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase mark autoimmune type 1 diabetes, not thyroiditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following normal thyroid structures is the source of the hormone now entering her circulation?
options: Calcitonin granules in parafollicular C cells
Lipid droplets in follicular cell cytoplasm
Dense-core granules at the apical cell surface
Colloid within the lumen of thyroid follicles
approach: High free T4 with almost no radioiodine uptake means the gland is not making new hormone.
The hormone must be coming from stores that leak out of inflamed, broken follicles.
Thyroid hormone is stored as part of thyroglobulin in the colloid that fills each follicle.
questions.why: Thyroid follicles are spheres of cuboidal follicular cells around a lumen filled with colloid. The colloid is mostly thyroglobulin, and T4 and T3 are stored on its iodinated tyrosines, enough to supply the body for weeks. Normally, follicular cells take up colloid by endocytosis and digest thyroglobulin in lysosomes to release hormone. In destructive thyroiditis, inflammation breaks the follicles, and stored thyroglobulin and hormone spill into the blood. Thyrotoxicosis lasts only until these stores run out. Parafollicular C cells sit between the follicles and store calcitonin, not thyroid hormone.
whyNot: Parafollicular C cells store calcitonin in secretory granules. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium and does not cause thyrotoxicosis.
Thyroid hormone is stored on a protein, not in lipid droplets. Lipid droplets are typical of steroid-making cells such as those of the adrenal cortex.
Thyroid hormone is not packed into dense-core secretory granules. These granules hold peptide hormones and amines in cells such as C cells and chromaffin cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three months later, her thyroid function is normal. She now takes an oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol. Her 8 AM serum total cortisol concentration is 31 μg/dL (5 to 23). She has no features of cortisol excess, and her plasma ACTH concentration is within the reference range. Which of the following best explains her total cortisol concentration?
options: Autonomous cortisol secretion by an adrenal adenoma
More cortisol-binding globulin with normal free cortisol
Ectopic ACTH secretion by an occult tumor
Increased ACTH release driven by residual thyroid hormone
approach: Estrogen raises hepatic synthesis of binding globulins, including cortisol-binding globulin and thyroxine-binding globulin.
More binding globulin holds more cortisol in the bound pool, so total cortisol rises.
Only free cortisol acts on tissues and feeds back on ACTH. With normal ACTH and no clinical signs, her free cortisol is normal.
questions.why: About 90% of plasma cortisol is bound, mostly to cortisol-binding globulin and the rest largely to albumin. Only free cortisol enters cells, binds the glucocorticoid receptor, and feeds back on CRH and ACTH. Estrogen from pregnancy or oral contraceptives raises cortisol-binding globulin. The brief fall in free cortisol raises ACTH until free cortisol is back to normal. The new steady state has a high total cortisol, a normal free cortisol, and a normal ACTH. The same logic explains a high total T4 with a normal free T4 when thyroxine-binding globulin rises.
whyNot: An autonomous adrenal adenoma secretes cortisol on its own and suppresses ACTH. Her ACTH is normal and she has no signs of cortisol excess.
Correct.
Ectopic ACTH secretion would raise plasma ACTH and cause clear signs of cortisol excess, often with hypokalemia.
Her thyroid function is now normal. Thyroid hormone excess speeds cortisol clearance and would not explain a high total cortisol with a normal ACTH.

topics: Effects of estrogen on total hormone levels

dx: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental maternal Graves antibodies
case: A 9-day-old girl is brought to the physician because of irritability, poor sleep, and sweating during feeds. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation. She feeds well but has not gained weight since birth. Her mother had Graves disease treated with radioactive iodine ablation 3 years ago and has taken levothyroxine since. The mother's thyroid tests were normal throughout pregnancy, but her thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin titer in the third trimester was more than three times the upper limit of normal. The infant's temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 205/min, and respirations are 52/min. She has a small diffuse goiter and mild proptosis. Serum TSH is undetectable, and free T4 is more than twice the upper limit of the reference range for age. The diagnosis is neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental maternal antibodies.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the infant is thyrotoxic while her mother is euthyroid?
options: Fetal B cells producing TSH receptor antibodies
Transfer of maternal levothyroxine across the placenta
Maternal IgM crossing the placenta into the fetus
Maternal IgG crossing the placenta through FcRn
approach: The mother's thyroid was destroyed by radioactive iodine, so her persisting antibodies have no thyroid to stimulate, and she stays euthyroid on replacement.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins are IgG, the only antibody class actively carried across the placenta, by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).
In the infant, these antibodies bind and activate TSH receptors on her own thyroid.
questions.why: Graves disease is caused by IgG antibodies that bind the TSH receptor and act like TSH, raising cAMP, hormone synthesis, and gland growth. It is classed as a type II hypersensitivity because the antibody targets a cell-surface antigen, here stimulating the cell instead of destroying it. Ablation or surgery removes the target tissue but not the B cells, so antibodies can persist for years. FcRn in the placenta transports maternal IgG to the fetus, mostly in the third trimester. High maternal titers can therefore cause fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis even when the mother is euthyroid. The disorder fades over weeks to a few months as maternal IgG is cleared.
whyNot: The fetus does not make its own TSH receptor antibodies. The antibodies came from the mother, which is why the disorder is transient.
Only small amounts of maternal levothyroxine cross the placenta, and her dose only keeps her own free T4 normal. Exogenous T4 would also suppress TSH and could not enlarge the infant's thyroid.
IgM is a large pentamer and does not cross the placenta. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins are IgG.
Correct.

questions.stem: If her thyrotoxicosis were to persist untreated for several months, which of the following skeletal effects would be most likely?
options: Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle
Premature fusion of the cranial sutures
Widened, frayed metaphyseal growth plates
Repeated fractures from abnormal type I collagen
approach: Thyroid hormone speeds bone turnover and skeletal maturation.
In adults, excess hormone causes net bone loss. In infants and children, it speeds maturation of growth centers, so bone age advances.
In an infant, early skeletal maturation can close the cranial sutures too soon (craniosynostosis).
questions.why: Thyroid hormone raises the metabolic rate of most tissues and increases sensitivity to catecholamines. This explains weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, tachycardia, and in adults atrial fibrillation. In bone, it increases both osteoblast and osteoclast activity, with resorption winning, so long-standing thyrotoxicosis in adults causes bone loss. In infants it also speeds skeletal maturation, advancing bone age and risking premature fusion of the cranial sutures. Untreated neonatal thyrotoxicosis can also cause heart failure, and in any age group a sudden, severe worsening (thyroid storm) is life-threatening.
whyNot: Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle is a sign of congenital hypothyroidism, the opposite state, in which skeletal maturation is slow.
Correct.
Widened, frayed growth plates are typical of rickets from vitamin D deficiency. Thyroid hormone excess does not impair mineralization in this way.
Repeated fractures from abnormal type I collagen point to osteogenesis imperfecta, an inherited collagen disorder unrelated to thyroid status.

topics: Effects of thyroid hormone on bone

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the development of the thyroid cells that are stimulated by the maternal antibodies?
options: Pharyngeal floor endoderm passing in front of the hyoid
Ultimobranchial body cells joining the lateral lobes
Stomodeal ectoderm growing upward toward the diencephalon
Third pouch endoderm descending with the thymus
approach: The antibodies bind TSH receptors, which are found on thyroid follicular cells.
Follicular cells come from an endodermal thickening in the floor of the primitive pharynx at the site of the future foramen cecum.
The gland then descends through the neck, attached for a time by the thyroglossal duct, passing in front of the hyoid bone to reach the front of the trachea.
questions.why: The thyroid is the first endocrine gland to develop, starting in about the fourth week as an endodermal outgrowth of the pharyngeal floor, between the anterior two thirds and posterior third of the future tongue. It descends in front of the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages to its final position, linked for a time to the tongue by the thyroglossal duct. The duct's upper opening remains as the foramen cecum. If descent fails, the gland may stay at the base of the tongue as a lingual thyroid. Parafollicular C cells come from neural crest cells that reach the gland through the ultimobranchial body, and they are not stimulated by TSH receptor antibodies.
whyNot: Correct.
The ultimobranchial body brings neural crest-derived C cells into the lateral lobes. These cells make calcitonin and are not the target of TSH receptor antibodies.
Ectoderm from the roof of the stomodeum forms Rathke pouch, which becomes the anterior pituitary.
Third pouch endoderm forms the thymus and the inferior parathyroid glands, which descend into the lower neck and chest.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions of thyroid hormone best explains her failure to gain weight despite good feeding?
options: Increased glucagon secretion raising glycogen breakdown
Reduced intestinal absorption of dietary fat
More Na/K-ATPase pumps, raising ATP use and heat
Leptin-driven activation of hypothalamic satiety
approach: She takes in enough calories but cannot store them, and she is sweating, so she is burning more energy than normal.
T3 binds nuclear receptors and increases transcription of Na/K-ATPase and other metabolic proteins.
More pumps use more ATP, raising oxygen consumption, basal metabolic rate, and heat production.
questions.why: Most T4 is converted to the more active T3 by deiodinases in peripheral tissues. T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors and changes gene transcription. It increases the number of Na/K-ATPase pumps in many tissues, so cells spend more ATP and consume more oxygen, raising the basal metabolic rate and heat production. It also increases lipolysis and protein turnover. The result is weight loss despite normal or increased intake, along with heat intolerance and sweating. Thyroid hormone also upregulates cardiac beta-1 receptors and is needed for normal bone growth and brain maturation.
whyNot: Thyroid hormone does not act mainly through glucagon, and a glucagon effect would not explain her sweating and heat production.
Thyroid hormone speeds gut transit and can cause frequent stools, but malabsorption is not the main reason for weight loss. Energy use rises even when absorption is normal.
Correct.
Leptin signals satiety and would reduce intake. She feeds well, so low intake is not the cause.

case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of palpitations, tremor, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss over 3 months. He grew up in a mountainous region where dietary iodine was low. His temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/74 mm Hg. A firm, nontender 3-cm nodule is palpable in the right thyroid lobe. The rest of the gland is not palpable. There is no proptosis or skin thickening. Serum TSH is below 0.01 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), and free T4 is 2.4 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8). A radioactive iodine scan shows intense uptake in the nodule and almost no uptake in the rest of the gland. The diagnosis is toxic adenoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the absent radioiodine uptake in the rest of his thyroid gland?
options: Suppression of TSH by hormone from the nodule
Destruction of normal follicles by lymphocytes
Blockade of TSH receptors by circulating antibodies
Compression of normal tissue by the enlarging nodule
approach: The nodule makes hormone on its own, usually because of an activating somatic mutation of the TSH receptor or of the Gs alpha subunit.
Its excess hormone suppresses pituitary TSH.
Normal follicles depend on TSH for iodide uptake, so without TSH they become inactive and look cold on the scan.
questions.why: Hyperthyroidism with low TSH and high free T4 has several causes, and the uptake scan helps tell them apart. In Graves disease, antibodies stimulate every follicle, so uptake is diffuse and increased, and eye and skin signs may be present. In toxic multinodular goiter, several autonomous nodules take up iodine in a patchy pattern, without eye or skin signs. In a toxic adenoma, one autonomous nodule takes up the tracer while the rest of the gland is suppressed. The suppressed tissue is normal and recovers after the nodule is removed and TSH returns.
whyNot: Correct.
Lymphocytic destruction occurs in Hashimoto and painless thyroiditis. It lowers uptake throughout the gland and would not leave one intensely active nodule.
TSH receptor-blocking antibodies occur in some autoimmune thyroid disease and cause hypothyroidism. They play no part in a toxic adenoma.
A 3-cm nodule does not compress the rest of the gland enough to stop its function. Low TSH, not pressure, silences the normal tissue.

questions.stem: At surgery, the right lobe is removed. To do this, the surgeon divides the narrow band of thyroid tissue that joins the two lobes across the midline. This band normally lies directly anterior to which of the following?
options: Arch of the cricoid cartilage
Laminae of the thyroid cartilage
Second and third tracheal rings
Fifth and sixth tracheal rings
approach: The narrow midline band that joins the lobes is the isthmus.
The lobes lie on either side of the larynx and upper trachea, and the isthmus crosses in front of the trachea.
The isthmus usually lies over the second and third tracheal rings, just below the cricoid cartilage.
questions.why: The thyroid gland has right and left lobes on the sides of the larynx and trachea, joined by an isthmus over the second and third tracheal rings. The gland is enclosed in pretracheal fascia, which attaches it to the larynx and trachea, so it rises with swallowing. The cricoid cartilage is a useful landmark, because the isthmus lies just below it. Surgeons divide the isthmus during a lobectomy, and it may need to be divided or retracted during a tracheostomy.
whyNot: The cricoid arch lies just above the isthmus and serves as the landmark for finding it.
The laminae of the thyroid cartilage lie higher, beside the upper parts of the lobes, not behind the isthmus.
Correct.
The fifth and sixth tracheal rings lie below the isthmus, in the lower neck toward the jugular notch.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how his childhood diet contributed to the development of his thyroid nodule?
options: Autoantibodies induced by poorly iodinated thyroglobulin
Prolonged TSH-driven growth of follicular cells
Increased deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3
Reduced calcitonin release from parafollicular cells
approach: Low iodine intake limits thyroid hormone synthesis.
Lower hormone output reduces negative feedback, so TSH rises and stimulates follicular cell growth for years.
Long-term stimulation causes goiter and nodules, and dividing cells can acquire mutations that make a nodule autonomous.
questions.why: Iodine is needed to iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin. When intake is low, hormone output falls, TSH rises, and the gland enlarges as a goiter, which keeps hormone levels near normal. Over many years, uneven growth produces nodules, and some clones acquire activating mutations of the TSH receptor or Gs that let them work without TSH. This is why toxic nodules and toxic multinodular goiter are more common in regions with low iodine intake. A sudden iodine load in such a person can then worsen hyperthyroidism, because the autonomous tissue makes as much hormone as the iodine supply allows.
whyNot: Autoantibodies drive Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis. Iodine deficiency is not their trigger, and a single hot nodule with suppressed surrounding tissue is not an antibody pattern.
Correct.
Deiodinases convert T4 to T3 and depend on selenium, not on iodine intake. Their activity does not cause follicular cell growth.
Calcitonin from C cells helps regulate calcium and has no role in follicular cell growth or goiter.

questions.stem: The radioactive iodide used for his scan was concentrated by the nodule. After iodide enters a follicular cell, in which of the following orders does hormone production occur?
options: Coupling, oxidation, organification, proteolysis
Organification, proteolysis, oxidation, coupling
Oxidation, proteolysis, organification, coupling
Oxidation, organification, coupling, proteolysis
approach: Iodide is trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter on the basal membrane and moves to the apical side.
Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin (organification), forming MIT and DIT, and then couples them into T3 and T4.
Hormone is released only when the cell takes colloid back in and lysosomal enzymes cleave thyroglobulin.
questions.why: The sodium-iodide symporter brings iodide into the follicular cell using the sodium gradient, and pendrin moves it into the follicle lumen. At the apical surface, thyroid peroxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize iodide and attach it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, forming monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT). The same enzyme couples two DIT to make T4, or MIT with DIT to make T3, still bound to thyroglobulin. To release hormone, the cell takes up colloid by endocytosis, lysosomal proteases cleave thyroglobulin, and T4 and T3 leave across the basolateral membrane.
whyNot: Coupling joins iodotyrosines, so it cannot happen before iodide has been oxidized and attached to thyroglobulin.
Organification needs oxidized iodine, so oxidation must come first. Proteolysis releases finished hormone and comes last.
Proteolysis of thyroglobulin releases finished T4 and T3. If it came before organification and coupling, there would be no hormone to release.
Correct.

dx: Primary thyroid lymphoma arising in Hashimoto thyroiditis
case: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless neck mass that has enlarged rapidly over the past 6 weeks, with hoarseness and difficulty swallowing solid food. She has had Hashimoto thyroiditis for 15 years, treated with levothyroxine. Her temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. A firm 7-cm mass replaces the right thyroid lobe and extends across the midline. Serum TSH is 2.1 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0). A core biopsy specimen shows sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells that express CD20, in a background of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. The diagnosis is primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the thyroid arising in Hashimoto thyroiditis.

questions.stem: In addition to lymphoma, this patient's thyroid disease places her at increased risk of which of the following disorders?
options: Hereditary hemochromatosis
Pernicious anemia
Pulmonary sarcoidosis
Systemic AL amyloidosis
approach: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an organ-specific autoimmune disease.
Patients with one organ-specific autoimmune disease have a higher risk of others because of shared genetic risk, such as HLA alleles and variants in immune regulatory genes.
Autoimmune gastritis with pernicious anemia is a classic association, along with type 1 diabetes, Addison disease, celiac disease, and vitiligo.
questions.why: Hashimoto thyroiditis often begins as a painless goiter. Some patients have a brief thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis) when follicles are first damaged, and most progress to permanent hypothyroidism as follicles are destroyed. Because it shares genetic risk with other autoimmune diseases, it often occurs with pernicious anemia, type 1 diabetes, Addison disease, and celiac disease. Together with Addison disease it forms autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2. Chronic lymphoid stimulation in the gland also raises the risk of primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma, which presents as a rapidly growing mass in an older woman with long-standing disease.
whyNot: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an HFE-related iron overload disorder. It is not autoimmune and is not linked to Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Correct.
Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease of unknown cause. It is not a recognized companion of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
AL amyloidosis comes from a plasma cell clone making light chains. Autoimmune thyroid disease does not predispose to it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the original loss of self-tolerance to thyroid antigens in this patient?
options: Molecular mimicry with streptococcal M protein
Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor
Direct viral infection of follicular epithelium
Gene variants that weaken T cell inhibition
approach: Hashimoto thyroiditis results from failure of self-tolerance to thyroid antigens such as thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin.
Susceptibility is linked to variants in immune regulatory genes, especially CTLA4 and PTPN22, along with certain HLA alleles.
Weaker inhibitory signaling lets self-reactive T cells escape control, enter the gland, and destroy follicles.
questions.why: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate. Polymorphisms in CTLA4, which delivers an inhibitory signal to T cells, and PTPN22, a phosphatase that limits T cell receptor signaling, weaken the brakes on self-reactive lymphocytes. Activated CD4+ T cells help CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill follicular cells, and interferon-gamma and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity add to the injury. The gland fills with lymphocytes and plasma cells forming germinal centers, follicles atrophy, and surviving follicular cells become Hürthle cells with pink, granular cytoplasm. The result is a painless goiter, most often in a middle-aged woman.
whyNot: Molecular mimicry with streptococcal M protein causes rheumatic fever, in which antibodies cross-react with heart antigens.
TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies cause Graves disease, which raises hormone output instead of destroying the gland.
A viral trigger is proposed for subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which causes a painful gland and usually resolves. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune disease.
Correct.

questions.stem: Ten years ago she had a nodule removed from the upper pole of her left thyroid lobe. After that operation, her speaking voice was normal at rest but tired easily, and she could no longer sing high notes. Injury to which of the following nerves most likely explains these voice changes?
options: Ansa cervicalis branch to the sternothyroid
Recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
approach: Loss of high pitch with a voice that tires points to paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal folds.
The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
This nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery at the upper pole, where it can be injured when the artery is ligated.
questions.why: The superior laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, divides into internal and external branches. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds. The external branch descends with the superior thyroid artery to supply the cricothyroid muscle, which tilts the thyroid cartilage forward and tenses the vocal folds for high-pitched sounds. Surgeons ligate the superior thyroid vessels close to the gland to spare it. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, in the tracheoesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery, supplies all the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and its injury causes a hoarse or breathy voice.
whyNot: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. Its injury does not change pitch or vocal fold tension.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyzes most intrinsic laryngeal muscles and causes a hoarse or breathy voice. The nerve is at risk near the lower pole and inferior thyroid artery, not the upper pole.
Correct.
The internal branch is sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds. Its injury impairs the cough reflex and raises the risk of aspiration but does not affect pitch.

topics: Nerves at risk in thyroid surgery

questions.stem: Her 41-year-old daughter has a slowly enlarging multinodular goiter and mild difficulty swallowing. The daughter's serum TSH and free T4 concentrations are within the reference ranges, and thyroid autoantibodies are absent. Which of the following best explains the daughter's normal thyroid function despite an enlarged gland?
options: Compensatory growth offsetting impaired hormone synthesis
Clonal neoplasm that secretes hormone without TSH control
Lymphocytic destruction balanced by follicular regrowth
Infiltration of the gland by calcitonin-derived amyloid
approach: A goiter with normal TSH and free T4 and no antibodies is a nontoxic (euthyroid) goiter.
It begins when hormone synthesis is mildly impaired, for example by low iodine intake, so TSH rises enough to make the gland grow until output is normal again.
Over years the follicles grow unevenly and form nodules, and a large gland can compress the esophagus or trachea.
questions.why: Nontoxic goiter is an enlarged thyroid without hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Mild impairment of hormone synthesis raises TSH a little, and follicular hyperplasia restores normal output, after which TSH settles back into the reference range. Repeated cycles of hyperplasia and involution produce a multinodular gland with hemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification. Symptoms come mainly from mass effect, such as dysphagia or airway compression. Most nodules in such a gland are benign, but a dominant nodule that is cold on radioiodine scan, grows quickly, or is fixed should be evaluated for a neoplasm.
whyNot: Correct.
A clonal neoplasm secreting hormone without TSH control is a toxic adenoma. It would suppress TSH and raise free T4.
Lymphocytic destruction with regrowth describes Hashimoto thyroiditis. Antibodies would usually be present, and function tends toward hypothyroidism.
Amyloid derived from calcitonin is a feature of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a tumor of C cells, not a cause of a multinodular goiter.

dx: Ectopic ACTH syndrome from a bronchial carcinoid tumor
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 9-kg (20-lb) weight gain, difficulty climbing stairs, and easy bruising over 6 months. She has never smoked. Her blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. Physical examination shows facial rounding, a dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple abdominal striae, and proximal muscle weakness. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0) and bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L (22 to 28). Twenty-four-hour urine free cortisol is 640 μg (less than 50), and plasma ACTH is 168 pg/mL (7 to 63). Cortisol does not suppress after high-dose dexamethasone. MRI of the pituitary gland is normal. CT of the chest shows a 1.8-cm nodule in the right lower lobe, and resection shows a typical carcinoid tumor that stains for ACTH. The diagnosis is ectopic ACTH syndrome from a bronchial carcinoid tumor.

questions.stem: If her Cushing syndrome had instead been caused by a cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma, which of the following sets of findings would be expected?
options: High ACTH with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
High ACTH that falls after high-dose dexamethasone
Low ACTH with atrophy of the opposite adrenal
Low ACTH with an adenoma in the pituitary gland
approach: An adrenal adenoma makes cortisol without ACTH, so it is an ACTH-independent cause.
Its cortisol suppresses CRH and ACTH, so plasma ACTH is low.
Without ACTH, the normal cortex atrophies, including the opposite adrenal gland.
questions.why: After hypercortisolism is confirmed, plasma ACTH is the next step. Low ACTH means an ACTH-independent cause: an adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, or exogenous glucocorticoids, which atrophy both adrenals. High or inappropriately normal ACTH means an ACTH-dependent cause: a pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH from a tumor such as small cell lung carcinoma or a bronchial carcinoid. In ACTH-dependent disease both adrenals become hyperplastic. High-dose dexamethasone usually suppresses a pituitary adenoma, which keeps some feedback sensitivity, but usually fails to suppress ectopic sources, as in this patient.
whyNot: High ACTH with bilateral hyperplasia is the pattern of ACTH-dependent disease, as in this patient, not of an adrenal adenoma.
High ACTH that falls with high-dose dexamethasone is the classic pattern of Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma.
Correct.
A pituitary corticotroph adenoma raises ACTH. Low ACTH rules out a pituitary source of cortisol excess.

questions.stem: Her plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration are both low. Which of the following best explains her hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis?
options: Cortisol exceeding the capacity of 11-beta-HSD type 2
Aldosterone secretion stimulated by excess ACTH
Renin release caused by cortisol-induced hypertension
Gain-of-function mutation in the collecting duct ENaC
approach: Low renin and low aldosterone mean the mineralocorticoid effect is not coming from aldosterone.

Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor about as well as aldosterone does. Renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 normally protects the receptor by converting cortisol to inactive cortisone.
Very high cortisol from ectopic ACTH overwhelms this enzyme, so cortisol activates the receptor and causes potassium and hydrogen ion loss.
questions.why: Mineralocorticoid receptors in collecting duct principal cells bind cortisol and aldosterone with similar affinity, yet plasma cortisol is far higher than aldosterone. The enzyme 11-beta-HSD2 protects the receptor by converting cortisol to cortisone. When cortisol is extremely high, as in ectopic ACTH syndrome, the enzyme is saturated and cortisol acts as a mineralocorticoid. This causes sodium retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with suppressed renin and aldosterone. For this reason hypokalemia is much more common in ectopic ACTH syndrome than in pituitary Cushing disease. Licorice produces a similar picture by inhibiting the enzyme.
whyNot: Correct.
ACTH has only a minor, short-lived effect on aldosterone secretion, and her aldosterone is low.
Hypertension suppresses renin rather than stimulating it, and her renin is low.
A gain-of-function ENaC mutation (Liddle syndrome) causes a similar electrolyte picture, but it is inherited and is not needed to explain her findings. Her very high cortisol fully accounts for them.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions of cortisol best explains her wide purple striae and easy bruising?
options: Androgen-driven thickening of the dermis
Impaired platelet aggregation
Sodium retention expanding the plasma volume
Reduced collagen synthesis by fibroblasts
approach: Striae and easy bruising both reflect thin, weak connective tissue in the skin and around small vessels.
Cortisol inhibits fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis and promotes protein breakdown.
The thin dermis tears as the abdomen enlarges, and poorly supported small vessels bruise easily.
questions.why: Cortisol is catabolic for connective tissue and muscle. It reduces collagen synthesis by fibroblasts and promotes protein breakdown, giving thin skin, wide purple striae, easy bruising, and poor wound healing. Breakdown of muscle protein supplies amino acids for gluconeogenesis and causes proximal muscle weakness. Cortisol also promotes lipolysis and central fat deposition, suppresses inflammation and immune responses, and is permissive for catecholamine vasoconstriction. Normally ACTH and cortisol peak in the early morning and fall to a low point near midnight.
whyNot: Androgens can thicken the skin and cause acne and hirsutism. They do not cause striae or bruising.
Cortisol excess does not impair platelet aggregation. The bruising comes from fragile, poorly supported vessels in thin skin.
Sodium retention adds to hypertension and weight but does not explain a thin, torn dermis.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man who smokes has a central lung mass and new confusion. His serum calcium is 13.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), and intact PTH is 6 pg/mL (10 to 65). A biopsy specimen of his tumor is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Small cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoid tumor
Lung adenocarcinoma
approach: High calcium with low phosphate and suppressed PTH means a PTH-like substance is acting while the parathyroid glands are shut down.
The usual cause is PTH-related peptide secreted by a tumor (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy).
In the lung, PTHrP secretion is most typical of squamous cell carcinoma, which is often central and strongly linked to smoking.
questions.why: Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes come from hormones made by tumors of tissues that are not normally endocrine. PTHrP binds the PTH receptor in bone and kidney, raising calcium and lowering phosphate, while the high calcium suppresses native PTH. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is a classic source, along with renal cell and breast carcinomas. Small cell carcinoma and some carcinoid tumors make ACTH, as in this patient's case, and small cell carcinoma also commonly makes ADH, causing SIADH.
whyNot: Small cell carcinoma is the classic source of ectopic ACTH and ADH, not PTHrP.
Correct.
Bronchial carcinoids can secrete ACTH, as in this patient, or serotonin. They are not a usual source of PTHrP.
Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall and is usually peripheral. It is a much less typical source of PTHrP than squamous cell carcinoma.

dx: Adrenocortical carcinoma with Cushing syndrome and virilization
case: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of rapid weight gain, increasing facial hair, acne, deepening of her voice, and absent menses over 5 months. Her blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg. Physical examination shows facial rounding, purple abdominal striae, coarse hair on the chin and upper lip, temporal balding, and clitoromegaly. Fasting serum glucose is 162 mg/dL (70 to 99). Twenty-four-hour urine free cortisol is 410 μg (less than 50), plasma ACTH is below 5 pg/mL (7 to 63), and serum DHEA sulfate is 1,450 μg/dL (35 to 430). CT shows an 11-cm heterogeneous left adrenal mass with necrosis, and tumor extends into the left adrenal vein. The diagnosis is adrenocortical carcinoma with Cushing syndrome and virilization.

questions.stem: Staging CT of a 70-year-old man with known lung carcinoma shows new masses in both adrenal glands that were not present 1 year earlier. Which of the following is the most likely nature of these masses?
options: Bilateral adrenocortical carcinoma
Bilateral pheochromocytoma
Bilateral adrenal myelolipoma
Metastatic lung carcinoma
approach: Compare how common each type of adrenal tumor is.
Metastases to the adrenal glands are far more common than primary adrenal cancer, and lung carcinoma is a frequent source.
New masses in both glands in a patient with a known primary cancer are most likely metastases.
questions.why: Adrenal cortical adenomas are common. They are usually small, well circumscribed, and yellow, and most are nonfunctional, though some secrete cortisol or aldosterone. Adrenocortical carcinoma is rare, usually large, invasive, and marked by hemorrhage and necrosis, and it often secretes several steroids. Cushing syndrome with virilization, as in this patient, strongly suggests carcinoma. Metastases are more common than primary adrenal carcinoma, and cancers of the lung and breast and melanoma often spread to the adrenals, frequently to both glands.
whyNot: Adrenocortical carcinoma is rare and almost always affects one gland. New masses in both glands in a patient with lung cancer are much more likely to be metastases.
Pheochromocytoma is bilateral mainly in hereditary syndromes such as MEN2. It is not the first explanation for new masses in a patient with known lung cancer.
Myelolipoma is an uncommon benign mix of fat and marrow elements, usually found by chance. It would not be expected to appear newly in both glands in this setting.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her serum DHEA sulfate concentration is markedly increased. Which of the following enzymes must be active in the tumor cells for them to produce DHEA from pregnenolone?
options: 21-Hydroxylase
17-alpha-Hydroxylase
11-beta-Hydroxylase
Aldosterone synthase
approach: DHEA is the main adrenal androgen, and her high DHEA sulfate shows the tumor is making it in excess.
All adrenal steroids start as cholesterol, which StAR moves into mitochondria, where side-chain cleavage forms pregnenolone.
To make androgens, pregnenolone must be hydroxylated at carbon 17 and then have its side chain cleaved. CYP17 does both (17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activity).
questions.why: Adrenal steroid synthesis branches from pregnenolone. Without 17-alpha-hydroxylation, pregnenolone goes through progesterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone, and corticosterone to aldosterone in the zona glomerulosa. With 17-alpha-hydroxylation, it goes to cortisol through 21- and 11-beta-hydroxylation in the zona fasciculata, or, with 17,20-lyase activity, to DHEA and androstenedione in the zona reticularis. Adrenocortical carcinomas often have inefficient late enzymes, so they release large amounts of precursors and androgens such as DHEA sulfate. A block of 17-alpha-hydroxylase lowers both cortisol and sex steroids and diverts precursors toward mineralocorticoids.
whyNot: 21-Hydroxylase acts on progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone on the way to aldosterone and cortisol. It is not needed to make DHEA.
Correct.
11-beta-Hydroxylase performs the last step to cortisol and corticosterone. It does not act in the androgen branch.
Aldosterone synthase works only in the zona glomerulosa, converting corticosterone to aldosterone.

questions.stem: Tumor thrombus is growing along the left adrenal vein. If it continues to extend in the direction of venous flow, it will next enter which of the following vessels?
options: Left renal vein
Inferior vena cava
Left gonadal vein
Left inferior phrenic vein
approach: Each adrenal gland drains through a single adrenal vein, and the two sides drain differently.
The right adrenal vein is very short and enters the inferior vena cava directly.
The left adrenal vein runs down to join the left renal vein, which then crosses in front of the aorta to the inferior vena cava.
questions.why: The adrenal glands receive three sets of arteries: superior adrenal arteries from the inferior phrenic arteries, middle adrenal arteries from the aorta, and inferior adrenal arteries from the renal arteries. Each gland drains through one vein. The left adrenal vein empties into the left renal vein, which also receives the left gonadal vein. The right adrenal vein is short and enters the inferior vena cava directly, which makes it harder to catheterize. Adrenal carcinomas can grow along these veins into the renal vein and inferior vena cava.
whyNot: Correct.
Only the right adrenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. On the left, blood reaches the vena cava through the left renal vein.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein beside the adrenal vein. Blood does not flow from the adrenal vein into it.
The left inferior phrenic vein usually drains into the left adrenal vein, so flow runs from it, not toward it.

topics: Blood supply of the adrenal glands

questions.stem: Before imaging, a late-night salivary cortisol test was used to screen for cortisol excess. Which of the following best explains why this test is useful for this purpose?
options: Saliva contains cortisol bound to its carrier globulin
Cortisol secretion normally peaks near midnight
Cortisol excess abolishes the normal nighttime low
Salivary glands convert cortisone to cortisol at night
approach: Cortisol secretion follows a daily rhythm, with a peak in the early morning and a low point near midnight.
In Cushing syndrome of any cause, this rhythm is lost, so late-night cortisol stays high.
Salivary cortisol reflects free plasma cortisol and is easy to collect at home at bedtime.
questions.why: Three screening tests are used for Cushing syndrome: 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, and the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Late-night testing works because ACTH and cortisol normally fall to their lowest level around midnight, and loss of this low point is an early, consistent feature of hypercortisolism. Saliva contains free cortisol, the active fraction, so the result is not affected by changes in binding globulin. Cortisol excess causes central obesity, moon facies, purple striae, proximal weakness, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and poor wound healing.
whyNot: Saliva contains free cortisol, not globulin-bound cortisol, which is one reason the test reflects the active hormone.
Cortisol normally peaks in the early morning, around waking, and is lowest near midnight.
Correct.
Salivary glands contain 11-beta-HSD2, which converts cortisol to cortisone, not the reverse.

dx: Primary aldosteronism from bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia
case: A 49-year-old man comes to the physician because his hypertension remains uncontrolled despite three medications. He has muscle cramps and nocturia. His blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg. There is no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show serum sodium 144 mEq/L (135 to 145), potassium 2.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (22 to 28). Plasma aldosterone is 26 ng/dL (4 to 21), and plasma renin activity is 0.2 ng/mL/h (0.5 to 4.0). Saline infusion does not suppress aldosterone. CT shows normal-appearing adrenal glands, and adrenal vein sampling shows equal aldosterone secretion from both sides. The diagnosis is primary aldosteronism from bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why he has no edema despite long-standing aldosterone excess?
options: Pressure natriuresis and natriuretic peptide release
Downregulation of mineralocorticoid receptors in the kidney
Hypokalemia blocking distal sodium reabsorption
Hepatic inactivation of most secreted aldosterone
approach: Aldosterone excess first causes sodium and water retention, expanding extracellular volume and raising blood pressure.
Higher arterial pressure and atrial stretch then increase renal sodium excretion through pressure natriuresis and atrial natriuretic peptide.
Sodium balance is restored at a slightly expanded volume (aldosterone escape), so edema does not develop, but potassium and hydrogen ion loss continue.
questions.why: In primary aldosteronism, autonomous aldosterone secretion from an adenoma (Conn syndrome) or bilateral hyperplasia increases sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct. The resulting volume expansion suppresses renin, so the pattern is hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin with high aldosterone. Within days, escape mechanisms limit further sodium retention, so serum sodium stays high-normal and edema is absent. Potassium secretion does not escape, so hypokalemia persists. In secondary hyperaldosteronism, as in renal artery stenosis, renin is high.
whyNot: Correct.
Mineralocorticoid receptors stay active, which is why potassium loss and alkalosis continue.
Hypokalemia does not block sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron, and aldosterone keeps driving ENaC activity.
Aldosterone is cleared mainly by the liver, but his plasma aldosterone is high, so clearance is not limiting its effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions of aldosterone in the collecting duct contributes most directly to his serum bicarbonate concentration?
options: Reduced ammonium excretion by principal cells
Increased bicarbonate secretion by beta intercalated cells
Increased H+ secretion by alpha intercalated cells
Decreased bicarbonate filtration at the glomerulus
approach: A high bicarbonate with hypokalemia and hypertension points to a metabolic alkalosis driven by mineralocorticoid excess.
Aldosterone stimulates the H+-ATPase of alpha intercalated cells, and the greater sodium reabsorption by principal cells makes the lumen more negative, which favors H+ and K+ secretion.
Each H+ secreted generates a new bicarbonate that returns to the blood.
questions.why: Aldosterone acts on collecting duct cells through the mineralocorticoid receptor. In principal cells it increases ENaC channels and basolateral Na/K-ATPase, so sodium reabsorption rises and the lumen-negative voltage drives potassium secretion through ROMK channels. In alpha intercalated cells it stimulates the H+-ATPase, so more acid is excreted and new bicarbonate is added to the blood. Hypokalemia adds to the alkalosis by shifting H+ into cells and increasing renal ammonium production. Aldosterone secretion is controlled mainly by angiotensin II and serum potassium, with ACTH playing only a minor role.
whyNot: Ammonium excretion rises, not falls, in hypokalemia, and principal cells are not the main site of ammonium handling. Less ammonium excretion would cause acidosis.
Beta intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate into the urine, which would lower serum bicarbonate.
Correct.
Bicarbonate is filtered freely, and aldosterone does not regulate its filtration.

topics: Actions of aldosterone in the collecting duct

questions.stem: If surgery on his adrenal glands were ever needed, a posterior approach through the back could reach them without entering the peritoneal cavity. Which of the following best explains this?
options: They are suspended in the lesser sac by a mesentery
They lie within renal fascia behind the peritoneum
They are enclosed within the transverse mesocolon
They are covered on all sides by visceral peritoneum
approach: The adrenal glands are retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall.
They sit superomedial to the kidneys inside the renal fascia, separated from the kidneys by fat and a thin layer of fascia.
A surgeon coming from the back passes through muscle and perirenal fat to reach them without opening the peritoneum.
questions.why: Each adrenal gland lies against the posterior abdominal wall within the renal fascia, on the upper medial part of the kidney. The right gland is pyramidal and lies behind the inferior vena cava, in contact with the bare area of the liver and the diaphragm. The left gland is crescent-shaped and lies along the medial border of the left kidney above the hilum, behind the stomach, pancreas, and splenic vessels. Because the glands are retroperitoneal, they can be reached through the back as well as through the abdomen.
whyNot: The lesser sac is a peritoneal space behind the stomach. The left adrenal gland lies behind its posterior wall, not suspended within it.
Correct.
The transverse mesocolon suspends the transverse colon. The adrenal glands lie far behind it on the posterior abdominal wall.
Organs covered on all sides by visceral peritoneum, such as the stomach or jejunum, are intraperitoneal. Reaching them requires entering the peritoneal cavity.

topics: Location and relations of the adrenal glands

questions.stem: If an adrenal gland from this patient were examined microscopically, which of the following regions would most likely show hyperplasia?
options: Long radial cords of pale, lipid-filled cells
Anastomosing cords of small cells beside the medulla
Large basophilic cells arranged around venous sinusoids
Rounded clusters of cells just below the capsule
approach: His disorder is excess aldosterone from both adrenal glands.
Aldosterone is made in the zona glomerulosa, the thin outermost layer of the cortex.
In this layer the cells form rounded clusters or arches just beneath the capsule.
questions.why: The adrenal cortex has three zones, each with a main product. The zona glomerulosa, under the capsule, has small cells in rounded clusters and makes aldosterone. The zona fasciculata, the thickest layer, has long radial cords of large cells whose lipid droplets make them look pale; it makes cortisol. The zona reticularis, next to the medulla, has a network of smaller cells, often containing lipofuscin, and makes adrenal androgens. The medulla contains chromaffin cells that store epinephrine and norepinephrine. In bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism, the zona glomerulosa of both glands is diffusely or micronodularly hyperplastic.
whyNot: Long cords of pale, lipid-filled cells form the zona fasciculata, which makes cortisol. His cortisol is not in excess.
Anastomosing cords of small cells next to the medulla form the zona reticularis, which makes adrenal androgens.
Large basophilic cells around venous sinusoids are chromaffin cells of the medulla, which make catecholamines.
Correct.

case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pubic hair and penile enlargement first noticed 8 months ago. He has grown 11 cm (4.3 in) in the past year, and his height is above the 97th percentile. His blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg, above the 99th percentile for his age and height. Examination shows Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, an enlarged penis, and testes 2 mL in volume bilaterally. Bone age is 8 years. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). Plasma renin activity is suppressed, and plasma ACTH, 11-deoxycortisol, and androstenedione concentrations are increased. Genetic testing shows two pathogenic CYP11B1 variants. The diagnosis is congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.

questions.stem: If his newborn sister had the same enzyme deficiency, which of the following findings would be most likely at birth?
options: Normal female genitalia with hypokalemia
Virilized external genitalia with a normal uterus
Virilized external genitalia with absent ovaries
Normal female genitalia with sex steroid deficiency
approach: In 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, cortisol is low, ACTH rises, and the blocked precursors are shunted to adrenal androgens.
In a 46,XX fetus, these androgens virilize the external genitalia during early development.
The ovaries and uterus form normally, because they depend on the absence of testes and anti-Müllerian hormone, not on adrenal steroids.
questions.why: Classic 21-hydroxylase and 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiencies both virilize affected girls before birth, causing clitoromegaly and labial fusion with normal internal female organs. They differ in mineralocorticoids. In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, aldosterone and 11-deoxycorticosterone are low, so salt wasting with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia can occur. In 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-deoxycorticosterone accumulates, so hypertension and hypokalemia occur instead, usually noticed later in childhood. In 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, sex steroids cannot be made, so girls have normal genitalia but do not enter puberty, and they have hypertension and hypokalemia.
whyNot: Hypokalemia with normal genitalia fits 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency. In 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, androgen excess virilizes a girl's genitalia, and hypertension and hypokalemia are usually not present at birth.
Correct.
Ovaries develop normally in congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Absent ovaries would point to a disorder of gonadal development, not an adrenal enzyme defect.
Sex steroid deficiency with normal female genitalia is the picture of 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, in which androgens and estrogens cannot be made.

topics: Comparison of the forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia

questions.stem: His parents are both healthy. His 7-year-old brother is unaffected. What is the probability that this brother is a heterozygous carrier of a CYP11B1 variant?
options: 1 in 4
1 in 2
2 in 3
3 in 4
approach: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is autosomal recessive, so both healthy parents are carriers.
A child of two carriers is affected (1 in 4), a carrier (2 in 4), or a noncarrier (1 in 4).
The brother is known to be unaffected, so only the three unaffected outcomes remain, and two of those three are carriers.
questions.why: All forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia are autosomal recessive. CYP21A2 mutations, causing 21-hydroxylase deficiency, account for about 90 to 95% of cases, and CYP11B1 mutations causing 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency are the next most common. Two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child with each pregnancy. When a sibling is already known to be unaffected, the affected outcome is removed, leaving a 2 in 3 chance that the sibling carries one mutant allele.
whyNot: 1 in 4 is the chance that any child of two carriers is affected, not the chance that an unaffected sibling is a carrier.
1 in 2 is the carrier chance for a child of two carriers before the child's status is known. Removing the affected outcome raises it.
Correct.
3 in 4 is the chance that a child of two carriers has at least one mutant allele, which counts affected children. This brother is known to be unaffected.

questions.stem: His adrenal glands are enlarged by hyperplasia of their steroid-producing tissue under chronic ACTH stimulation. This tissue develops from which of the following embryonic sources?
options: Neural crest cells from the thoracic neural tube
Endoderm of the dorsal foregut wall
Surface ectoderm of the dorsal body wall
Mesoderm lining the posterior abdominal wall
approach: Chronic ACTH drive enlarges the adrenal cortex, the steroid-producing part of the gland.
The cortex develops from mesoderm, from cells of the coelomic epithelium lining the posterior abdominal wall near the developing gonads.
The medulla, which makes catecholamines, comes from neural crest cells that invade the developing cortex.
questions.why: The adrenal gland has two embryonic sources. The cortex arises from mesoderm (coelomic mesothelium) next to the urogenital ridge, which is why adrenal and gonadal cells share steroid-making machinery and why adrenal rest tissue can occur in the testes. Neural crest cells migrate into the cortex to form the medulla, whose chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons. Tumors of neural crest origin, such as pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, arise in the medulla, while the ACTH-driven hyperplasia of congenital adrenal hyperplasia affects the cortex.
whyNot: Neural crest cells form the adrenal medulla, not the cortex. The medulla does not respond to ACTH with hyperplasia.
Foregut endoderm forms the lining of the gut and organs such as the liver and pancreas, not the adrenal cortex.
Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis and its appendages. It does not contribute to the adrenal gland.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best distinguishes his precocious puberty from central precocious puberty?
options: Testes of prepubertal size
Bone age ahead of chronological age
Rapid gain in height over the past year
Pubic hair with penile enlargement
approach: Central precocious puberty is early activation of hypothalamic GnRH, which raises LH and FSH.
LH and FSH stimulate the testes, so testicular enlargement is the hallmark of central puberty in boys.
In peripheral precocious puberty, as in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the androgens come from the adrenal glands, LH and FSH are suppressed, and the testes stay small.
questions.why: In central precocious puberty, the whole hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis switches on early. LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone, and FSH drives growth of the seminiferous tubules, so the testes enlarge beyond 4 mL. In peripheral precocious puberty, sex steroids come from a source that does not depend on GnRH, such as the adrenal glands in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a sex steroid-secreting tumor, or McCune-Albright syndrome. Feedback from these steroids suppresses LH and FSH, so the testes stay prepubertal in size while virilization, fast growth, and advanced bone age occur.
whyNot: Correct.
Advanced bone age results from sex steroids of any source, so it occurs in both central and peripheral precocious puberty.
Rapid linear growth results from sex steroid exposure and occurs in both forms.
Androgens from either the testes or the adrenal glands cause pubic hair and penile growth, so these findings do not separate the two forms.

case: An 8-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of poor feeding, irritability, constipation, and poor weight gain. His parents report that he cries for water, drinks eagerly, and soaks his diapers. He has had several unexplained fevers. A maternal uncle had similar problems as an infant. He is at the 3rd percentile for weight. His temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 34/min. His mucous membranes are dry. Serum sodium is 154 mEq/L (135 to 145), and serum osmolality is 312 mOsm/kg H2O (275 to 295). Urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg H2O. Plasma copeptin, a marker of ADH secretion, is markedly increased. Genetic testing shows a pathogenic AVPR2 variant. The diagnosis is X-linked congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

questions.stem: In adults, the same type of renal resistance to ADH can be acquired. Which of the following metabolic disorders is a recognized cause?
options: Hyperkalemia
Hypermagnesemia
Hypercalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
approach: His disorder is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: the kidney cannot respond to ADH, so urine stays dilute despite high ADH.
Acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus comes from drugs such as lithium and from electrolyte disorders that impair the collecting duct response.
Hypercalcemia and hypokalemia both reduce urine concentrating ability.
questions.why: Diabetes insipidus means the passage of large volumes of dilute urine because ADH action fails. In central diabetes insipidus, ADH is not made or released, as after head trauma, pituitary surgery, or tumors. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, ADH is present but the kidney does not respond. Congenital forms come from mutations in the V2 receptor (X-linked, about 90% of inherited cases) or in aquaporin-2. Acquired forms come from lithium, hypercalcemia, and hypokalemia, which reduce aquaporin-2 expression and the medullary concentration gradient. Both types cause polyuria and thirst, and hypernatremia develops when access to water is limited, as in infants.
whyNot: Hyperkalemia does not impair urine concentration. It is hypokalemia that causes acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Hypermagnesemia is not a recognized cause of renal resistance to ADH.
Correct.
Hyperphosphatemia is not a recognized cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

questions.stem: His 19-year-old male cousin has the same variant. If the cousin had a supervised water deprivation test followed by desmopressin, which of the following urine osmolality responses would be expected?
options: Little rise with deprivation and little rise after desmopressin
Little rise with deprivation and a large rise after desmopressin
Large rise with deprivation and no further rise after desmopressin
Large rise with deprivation and a large further rise after desmopressin
approach: Water deprivation raises plasma osmolality, which should release ADH and concentrate the urine.
Desmopressin then shows whether the kidney can respond to ADH.
In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, endogenous ADH is high but ineffective, so urine stays dilute after deprivation and after desmopressin.
questions.why: The water deprivation test separates three causes of polyuria. In primary polydipsia, ADH release and the kidney response are normal, so urine concentrates with deprivation and changes little after desmopressin. In central diabetes insipidus, urine stays dilute during deprivation because ADH is lacking, then concentrates sharply after desmopressin. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, urine stays dilute throughout, because the V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 pathway does not work. The test is supervised closely and stopped if the patient loses too much weight or becomes hypernatremic.
whyNot: Correct.
Little rise with deprivation followed by a large rise after desmopressin is the pattern of central diabetes insipidus, in which ADH is missing but the kidney can respond.
A large rise with deprivation and little change after desmopressin is the pattern of primary polydipsia or a healthy person.
A kidney that cannot respond to ADH cannot concentrate urine at either step, so this pattern does not fit his disorder.

questions.stem: In a healthy infant, binding of ADH to the receptor that is defective in this patient leads to which of the following events in collecting duct principal cells?
options: IP3-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum
Insertion of aquaporin-1 into the apical membrane
Opening of ROMK potassium channels in the apical membrane
Apical insertion of aquaporin-2 via cAMP
approach: The defective receptor in X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the V2 receptor on collecting duct principal cells.
The V2 receptor is coupled to Gs, so ADH raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A.
Protein kinase A moves vesicles carrying aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane, so water can follow the medullary osmotic gradient.
questions.why: ADH is released from the posterior pituitary when hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a small rise in plasma osmolality and, more strongly, when baroreceptors sense a large fall in blood volume or pressure. In the kidney, ADH binds V2 receptors on principal cells, activating Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A. Aquaporin-2 water channels move from intracellular vesicles into the apical membrane, and water leaves the cell through basolateral aquaporin-3 and aquaporin-4 into the hypertonic interstitium. V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle use Gq and IP3 to cause vasoconstriction.
whyNot: IP3 and calcium release make up the V1 receptor pathway, which constricts vascular smooth muscle. It is not the V2 response in principal cells.
Aquaporin-1 is always present in the proximal tubule and thin descending limb and is not regulated by ADH. ADH acts on principal cells through aquaporin-2.
ROMK channels secrete potassium and are increased by aldosterone and high distal flow, not by the V2 receptor.
Correct.

topics: Regulation and renal action of ADH

questions.stem: ADH is made in hypothalamic neurons as part of a larger precursor molecule. Which of the following is cleaved from this same precursor and carries ADH down the axons to the posterior pituitary?
options: Neurophysin I
Neurophysin II
Proopiomelanocortin
Chromogranin A
approach: ADH is made mainly in the supraoptic nucleus, and also in the paraventricular nucleus, as a preprohormone.
The precursor contains ADH, its carrier neurophysin II, and copeptin, which are packaged together in secretory granules.
The granules travel down axons in the pituitary stalk to the posterior pituitary, where they are stored and released.
questions.why: The posterior pituitary is an extension of the hypothalamus. Large neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin as larger precursors. The ADH precursor yields ADH, neurophysin II, and copeptin, and the oxytocin precursor yields oxytocin and neurophysin I. Each neurophysin binds its hormone inside secretory granules during axonal transport and is released with it. Mutations in the gene for the ADH and neurophysin II precursor cause familial central diabetes insipidus. In this patient, ADH production is normal, which is why copeptin is high, but the kidney cannot respond.
whyNot: Neurophysin I is the carrier for oxytocin and is cleaved from the oxytocin precursor.
Correct.
Proopiomelanocortin is the precursor of ACTH, MSH, and beta-endorphin in anterior pituitary corticotrophs.
Chromogranin A is a general protein of neuroendocrine secretory granules. It is not part of the ADH precursor.

dx: Primary empty sella syndrome with partial hypopituitarism
case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, cold intolerance, and irregular menses for 1 year. She has chronic headaches. She has no history of obstetric hemorrhage, head injury, pituitary surgery, or radiation. Her BMI is 38 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.4 °C (97.5 °F), pulse is 58/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows mild bilateral papilledema. Visual fields are full. Serum TSH is 1.0 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 is 0.6 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), LH and FSH are low-normal, estradiol is low, and prolactin is 31 ng/mL (less than 25). MRI shows a sella turcica filled with cerebrospinal fluid and a thin rim of pituitary tissue along its floor. The diagnosis is primary empty sella syndrome with partial hypopituitarism.

questions.stem: Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of her empty sella?
options: Ischemic necrosis of an enlarged gland after delivery
Hemorrhage into a preexisting pituitary adenoma
Granulomatous infiltration of the pituitary stalk
Raised CSF pressure acting through the diaphragma
approach: With no history of hemorrhage, surgery, or radiation, this is a primary empty sella, not a secondary one.
Primary empty sella occurs when arachnoid and CSF herniate through an incompetent diaphragma sellae.
Her obesity, headaches, and papilledema point to raised intracranial pressure, which pushes CSF into the sella and flattens the gland.
questions.why: Hypopituitarism has many causes: compression by a nonfunctioning macroadenoma, Sheehan necrosis after postpartum hemorrhage, pituitary apoplexy, surgery or radiation, and infiltrative or inflammatory disease. Primary empty sella syndrome results from a defect in the diaphragma sellae that lets arachnoid and CSF herniate into the sella. CSF pulsations, made worse by raised intracranial pressure such as idiopathic intracranial hypertension in obese women, flatten the pituitary against the floor of the sella. Most people with an empty sella have normal pituitary function, but some develop partial hypopituitarism or mild hyperprolactinemia. A secondary empty sella follows destruction of the gland by infarction, apoplexy, surgery, or radiation.
whyNot: Postpartum ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome) causes a secondary empty sella. She has no history of obstetric hemorrhage.
Hemorrhage into an adenoma (pituitary apoplexy) causes sudden severe headache, often with visual loss, and leaves a secondary empty sella. Her course is gradual, with no known adenoma.
Granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis thickens the stalk and often causes diabetes insipidus. It does not by itself empty the sella.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her visual fields are full. If a pituitary macroadenoma had instead grown upward out of the sella, which of the following visual field defects would be most likely?
options: Left homonymous hemianopia
Bitemporal hemianopia
Binasal hemianopia
Right monocular blindness
approach: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica beneath the diaphragma sellae, and the optic chiasm lies just above it.
A tumor growing upward presses on the middle of the chiasm from below.
The crossing fibers in the chiasm come from the nasal halves of both retinas, which see the temporal fields, so both temporal fields are lost.
questions.why: The sella turcica of the sphenoid bone holds the pituitary. Its roof is the diaphragma sellae, a fold of dura with an opening for the stalk. The optic chiasm lies above the diaphragma, and the cavernous sinuses, containing the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, lie on either side. Upward extension of a tumor compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibers and causes bitemporal hemianopia, often starting in the upper temporal fields. In empty sella syndrome the gland is flattened downward, so the chiasm is usually spared.
whyNot: A homonymous hemianopia comes from a lesion behind the chiasm, such as in the optic tract or radiations, not from midline compression.
Correct.
Binasal defects require pressure on the uncrossed lateral fibers of both sides. They are rare and not typical of pituitary tumors.
Monocular blindness comes from a lesion of one optic nerve in front of the chiasm.

questions.stem: Her low free T4 with a TSH that is not raised reflects inadequate stimulation of her thyrotrophs. Normally, TRH released by hypothalamic neurons reaches thyrotrophs by which of the following routes?
options: Median eminence capillaries, portal veins, anterior lobe sinusoids
Axons in the stalk, posterior lobe capillaries, anterior lobe cells
Third ventricle fluid, diaphragma sellae, anterior lobe cells
Inferior hypophyseal arteries, posterior lobe, cavernous sinus
approach: Hypothalamic releasing hormones are secreted from nerve endings in the median eminence, not carried into the anterior lobe by axons.
Superior hypophyseal arteries, branches of the internal carotid artery, form a capillary plexus in the median eminence that picks up these hormones.
Portal veins along the stalk carry this blood to a second capillary bed, the sinusoids of the anterior lobe.
questions.why: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system links two capillary beds in series. Releasing hormones such as TRH, CRH, GnRH, and GHRH, and also dopamine, enter the first bed in the median eminence and reach the anterior lobe at high concentration in portal blood. Most of the anterior lobe's blood arrives through these low-pressure portal veins rather than directly from arteries, which makes the lobe vulnerable to ischemic necrosis during hypotension, especially when it is enlarged in pregnancy. The posterior lobe has its own arterial supply from the inferior hypophyseal arteries.
whyNot: Correct.
Axonal transport to the posterior lobe is the route for ADH and oxytocin. Hypothalamic releasing hormones do not reach the anterior lobe this way.
Releasing hormones are not delivered to the pituitary through cerebrospinal fluid.
The inferior hypophyseal arteries supply mainly the posterior lobe, and the cavernous sinus receives venous drainage from the gland. This path does not carry hypothalamic hormones to thyrotrophs.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man has heat intolerance, palpitations, a diffuse goiter, and a pituitary macroadenoma on MRI. Which of the following patterns of serum TSH and free T4 is most likely in this man?
options: Suppressed TSH and low free T4
Suppressed TSH and high free T4
Elevated TSH and high free T4
Elevated TSH and low free T4
approach: Heat intolerance, palpitations, and a goiter in a man with a pituitary macroadenoma suggest a TSH-secreting adenoma.
The tumor secretes TSH without normal feedback, so TSH is high or inappropriately normal while free T4 is high.

Compare this with central hypothyroidism, as in the woman in the case, with low free T4 and a TSH that is low or inappropriately normal, and with primary hypothyroidism, with high TSH and low free T4.
questions.why: Reading TSH and free T4 together locates a thyroid disorder. Primary hypothyroidism has high TSH and low free T4, because the pituitary responds to low hormone. Central hypothyroidism, from pituitary or hypothalamic disease, has low free T4 with a TSH that is low or inappropriately normal. Graves disease and other thyroid sources of hyperthyroidism have suppressed TSH and high free T4. A TSH-secreting adenoma is the rare case with high free T4 and a TSH that is high or not suppressed. In primary hypothyroidism, raised TRH can also stimulate prolactin release, causing menstrual disturbance and infertility.
whyNot: Suppressed TSH with low free T4 fits central hypothyroidism, not a tumor causing hyperthyroidism.
Suppressed TSH with high free T4 is the pattern when the thyroid itself is the source of excess hormone, as in Graves disease.
Correct.
Elevated TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism, which causes cold intolerance, not heat intolerance.
